API keys are available for clients that cannot complete OAuth; they are scoped, revocable, displayed only when created, and should be stored as credentials.

Integration permissions separate three capabilities:

| Scope       | Capability                                                      |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Read**    | Inspect accessible drawings and their project context           |
| **Write**   | Change drawing records, charter data, issues, and related state |
| **Execute** | Run supported Python or SQL jobs against an accessible drawing  |

These scopes do not bypass drawing or organization permissions. The connected identity must also have the access required for the requested operation. Cloud Python execution additionally requires an entitled paid plan in the drawing’s organization.

***

## What an Agent Can Do [#what-an-agent-can-do]

Scopture’s MCP tools cover five functional areas:

* **Orient** — identify the active drawing, current application context, visible state, and available drawings.
* **Inspect** — search elements, read drawing records, retrieve external files, inspect versions, and capture screenshots.
* **Trace** — read and maintain the charter, requirements, constraints, decisions, issues, and issue messages.
* **Change** — create or update drawing content and switch application modes when an operation requires focused model interaction.
* **Compute and recover** — run Python or SQLite work, export assets, inspect job results, and restore a known version or automated change boundary.

Tool descriptions and input schemas are the authoritative reference for individual operations. They remain closer to the running service than a static copy of every argument in this documentation.

### MCP and CLI Coverage [#mcp-and-cli-coverage]

Remote CLI commands and MCP tools use the same validated backend operations and resource permissions. Protocol response envelopes differ; the underlying operations are shared.

| Capability                        | CLI                                              | MCP                                                        |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Create/list/read drawings         | `drawing create/list/get`                        | `create_drawing`, `list_available_drawings`, `get_drawing` |
| Inspect/filter elements and files | `elements`, `cat`, `files`                       | `get_elements`, `get_external_files`                       |
| Canvas/model images and exports   | `render`, `export`                               | `get_drawing_screenshot`, `export_asset`                   |
| Python and SQL                    | `run-python`, `run-sql`                          | `run_python_code`, `run_sqlite`, `check_python_run_job`    |
| Issue lifecycle                   | `issues list/create/update/close/reopen/dismiss` | `list_issues`, `create_issues`, `update_issue`             |
| Charter inspection                | `charter get`                                    | `get_charter`                                              |

For an inline rendered image, call `get_drawing_screenshot` with `viewport: { x, y, width, height }` in scene coordinates, or `elementId` plus `viewConfig` for model camera/display/clipping settings. Output `width`/`height` are pixels. No open client is required. `export_asset` supplies image/vector/CAD files as short-lived download URLs; it accepts the same viewport/view settings and STL `meshOptions`.

Download presigned URLs with HTTP **GET**. Their signatures authorize that method; a **HEAD** request can return 403 even when downloading with GET succeeds.

MCP additionally exposes Issue messages, user lookup, charter changes, version inspection/recovery, server text search and live model-mode commands. Saved checkpoints and deltas can be restored without an open client, preserving current Issues and charter and recording a rollback version. The CLI has no dedicated commands for those operations. Structural comparison of local or remote drawings, OS file destinations, desktop focus, offline drawings and local sandbox execution remain CLI capabilities.

Neither interface exposes deletion of Issues or Charter items. The user must delete them manually in Scopture. Use close or dismiss when that is the intended Issue action; SQL and Python drawing updates preserve existing Issue and message identities.

***

## Execution Model [#execution-model]

An effective agent workflow is:

1. Resolve the drawing and inspect its current context.
2. Retrieve only the records and external assets needed for the task.
3. Perform a narrow calculation, query, or edit.
4. Poll asynchronous Python or SQL work instead of submitting the same job again.
5. Verify the result through the updated records, a drawing screenshot, or Model Open mode.
6. Leave the automatic version delta as the recoverable boundary for the operation.

The remote MCP server operates on remote drawings. Local `.duc` files and native file links stay on the device and are not sent to remote execution. Use the [desktop CLI](/docs/automation/cli-tool) for terminal access to a local drawing.

***

## Python and SQLite [#python-and-sqlite]

The Python environment is an isolated Python 3.12 sandbox with Duc-aware drawing helpers and engineering libraries including NumPy, SciPy, SymPy, Pint, pandas, Matplotlib, and Fluids. It can read the current `.duc` data, resolve referenced files, perform engineering calculations, and submit drawing changes.

Model source declares one typed artifact with `emit_output(...)`. Its envelope identifies the renderer, MIME type, content hash, code and input fingerprints, and runtime version. This contract supports parametric 3D, IFC, DXF, image, SVG, PDF, and table outputs. A returned artifact is separate from a drawing mutation: use drawing updates when the operation must change the Model Element or its referenced files. See [Model Elements](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/elements/model-element) for the API and persistence fields.

For an IfcOpenShell model, use `emit_output(ifc_model, kind="ifc")` to retain the IFC file and its IFC renderer. `show(ifc_model)` uses the default parametric capture and does not declare an IFC artifact.

Drawing updates use **patch semantics**. The update should contain only records that were added or changed:

* an existing ID updates the corresponding record;
* a new ID adds a record;
* omitted records remain unchanged; and
* an element is deleted by updating its `is_deleted` field to `true`.

It is therefore unnecessary—and undesirable—to fetch, rewrite, and submit the complete drawing for a localized change.

SQLite jobs provide direct structured access to the `.duc` database through the supported Duc query layer. Use them for targeted inspection or mutation when the task is naturally relational. Use Python when the task requires calculations, geometry generation, external-file processing, or multi-step drawing logic.

See the [SQLite Runner](/docs/automation/sqlite-runner) for per-drawing queries, attached databases, mutations, and asynchronous job handling.

<Callout type="warn" title="Prefer the narrowest valid mutation">
  Read the current state before writing, preserve existing IDs and relationships, and submit only the intended patch. Automated changes are versioned, but a recoverable history is not a substitute for a well-scoped operation.
</Callout>

***

## Verification and Recovery [#verification-and-recovery]

A successful tool response proves that an operation completed, not that the resulting drawing communicates the intended outcome. Agents should inspect the changed records and use a screenshot or interactive model view when visual placement or geometry matters.

Scopture records agent operations as automatic deltas in the drawing’s version graph. Those boundaries can be inspected and restored without treating automation as an opaque side channel.

For the underlying `.duc` storage and element model, see the [Duc documentation](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/).


# Python Sandbox (/ar/docs/automation/python-sandbox)



Scopture’s Python sandbox runs Model Elements and drawing automation in a managed **Python 3.12** environment. Use it to compute geometry, analyse engineering models, produce visual results and apply deliberate drawing updates.

## Where Code Runs [#where-code-runs]

* **Desktop:** the installed local sandbox is the default for both local and remote drawings, including background output and thumbnail generation. Remote drawing access still requires authorization.
* **CLI:** `scopture run-python` uses the installed desktop sandbox when available, including for remote IDs. Pass `--server` to request cloud execution explicitly.
* **Browser and mobile:** an authorized cloud drawing on an entitled paid plan uses the server worker. Offline Python execution requires desktop.

Desktop and server derive their dependencies from the same sandbox `pyproject.toml` and lockfile and use the same worker implementation. Native wheels, operating-system libraries and graphics backends still require platform-specific verification.

Desktop jobs wait in a local queue. Up to four workers run at once, reduced according to available CPU and memory while reserving resources for the app. Queued jobs do not fail just because all worker slots are occupied.

The desktop installer includes uv and a locked runtime profile. First preparation installs Python and its dependencies into Scopture’s user storage. Later launches reuse the prepared environment offline; updates reuse unchanged environments and [uv’s package cache](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/cache/). Scopture does not install packages into your host Python or use arbitrary user site-packages. Development uses the workspace `ducpy`; distribution builds resolve and lock the published version when packaging.

## Two Execution Contexts [#two-execution-contexts]

A **Model Element** runs its Python source and imports drawing-local dependencies. Its output is a persisted artifact, separate from its source and thumbnail. Saved output can be viewed without re-executing the model.

A **drawing-level job**, invoked through the CLI or MCP, receives a drawing snapshot and can inspect or patch the document. Reading the drawing and emitting an output do not themselves modify it: call `update_drawing(...)` for an intended change.

### Submitting and Polling Jobs [#submitting-and-polling-jobs]

MCP `run_python_code` returns a `jobId`; `waitForCompletionMs` defaults to `0`. Submit once and poll that ID with `check_python_run_job` until it completes or fails. Each polling call waits at most 20 seconds, even when a longer wait is requested. A pending response is not a failed job: do not rerun pending code, particularly mutations. The CLI handles remote job polling for `run-python` and `run-sql`.

Import installed libraries explicitly and declare model output:

```python
from build123d import Box
emit_output(Box(20, 10, 5), kind="parametric")
```

## Embedded Methods and Values [#embedded-methods-and-values]

| Interface                                                   | Purpose                                                                                                                                               |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `emit_output(value, kind=..., mime_type=..., filename=...)` | Declare the rendering root’s output. Use one output per root.                                                                                         |
| `show(*objects, **options)`                                 | Compatibility helper for supported CAD/IFC objects, including `ocp_vscode.show`. Prefer explicit `emit_output` for new scripts.                       |
| `get_drawing()`                                             | Return current `.duc` bytes when the job has a drawing snapshot; it is not a drawing metadata dictionary.                                             |
| `update_drawing(patch)`                                     | Serialize and validate an intended drawing patch, then merge records by ID. Omitted records remain. Rendering and export jobs reject drawing updates. |
| `get_external_files(*file_ids)`                             | Return a dictionary of mounted file IDs to byte payloads.                                                                                             |
| `resolve_external_file(file_id)`                            | Return the mounted workspace path for a file ID.                                                                                                      |
| `external_files`                                            | Mounted file metadata indexed by ID; entries include a workspace `path`.                                                                              |
| `drawing_files`                                             | Drawing file metadata supplied to the job.                                                                                                            |
| `FontEnum([...])`                                           | Declare a font selection parameter with iteration, key access, and identifier-safe attributes.                                                        |
| `resolve_font(family)`                                      | Return a mounted font’s local TTF path for libraries requiring a filename.                                                                            |
| `duc_model.<stable-module-name>`                            | Import values and functions from another Python Model Element in this drawing.                                                                        |

File helpers only expose inputs mounted for the current job. Drawing snapshot helpers require that context; do not assume a standalone Model Element run receives a complete drawing file.

`ducpy.parse_duc()` is path-based. To inspect snapshot bytes, write them to a workspace `.duc` path and parse that path. Use `ducpy`’s installed API reference for builders and serialization, rather than assuming sandbox helper names are `ducpy` methods.

### Fonts [#fonts]

```python
FONTS = FontEnum(["Noto Sans", "Roboto"])
family = FONTS.Noto_Sans  # also FONTS["Noto Sans"] or iteration over FONTS
font_path = resolve_font(family)
```

The selected TTF must be mounted for the job; declaring a name does not install a font. `resolve_font` raises an error when that family is unavailable. `build123d.Text(..., font=family)` resolves the mounted TTF automatically; other libraries can use the returned path directly.

## Output Contract [#output-contract]

| `kind`       | Viewer/output                                             |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `parametric` | Supported B-Rep/mesh objects or a tessellated CAD preview |
| `ifc`        | IFC model                                                 |
| `dxf`        | DXF drawing                                               |
| `image`      | Raster image bytes or a workspace image path              |
| `svg`        | SVG markup/bytes or a workspace SVG path                  |
| `pdf`        | PDF bytes or a workspace PDF path                         |
| `table`      | Structured table data                                     |

A logic-only parameter/helper module needs no output. Imported dependencies’ `show(...)` and `emit_output(...)` calls do not replace the root output. HTML and video are not Model Element output kinds; keep them as explicit file assets where appropriate. See the [Model Element output contract](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/elements/model-element) for supported values and envelope details.

```python
import io
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

force_n = 80.0
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.plot([0, 1, 2], [0, force_n / 2, force_n])
ax.set(xlabel="Time / s", ylabel="Force / N")
output = io.BytesIO()
fig.savefig(output, format="png")
plt.close(fig)
emit_output(output.getvalue(), kind="image", mime_type="image/png", filename="force.png")
```

## Reuse Geometry in Simulations [#reuse-geometry-in-simulations]

Keep the mechanical model in one Model Element. Import its actual solids, meshes, dimensions or functions from each study, then emit that study’s own image or table. Avoid copying the source assembly into every simulation.

Use the editor’s import completion to insert the stable module name; IDs containing punctuation use an encoded `element_...` name. Labels are readable aliases only when unambiguous. See [Model Parameters](/docs/concepts/model-parameters) and [Model Modularization](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/model-modularization).

```python
# In a study; replace the module name with the source model's stable name.
from duc_model.geometry import shaft, shaft_diameter
```

In this example the source Model Element must have the stable ID `geometry` and export both names. Prefer reusable definitions and values in shared modules; each consuming study owns its calculation assumptions and output.

## Drawing Updates [#drawing-updates]

Submit complete valid changed records with `update_drawing({"elements": [...]})`. The helper accepts a state dictionary, a compatible `ducpy` object, or valid `.duc` bytes. Dictionary and object inputs are serialized with embedded-code validation. Matching IDs update existing records, new IDs add records, and omitted records remain unchanged. Preserve existing IDs and memberships; do not submit the entire drawing merely to change one item. Inspect the result, then render it for visual QA.

## Capability mapping [#capability-mapping]

| Capability                               | Expected result                                                               | Python package(s)                                 |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| CAD solids / STEP                        | Parametric geometry, B-Rep, STEP import/export                                | `build123d, cadquery-ocp`                         |
| BIM / IFC                                | Building objects and properties                                               | `ifcopenshell`                                    |
| 2D CAD / DXF                             | Layers, blocks, entities and drawings                                         | `ezdxf`                                           |
| Mesh generation                          | Surface/volume mesh, B-Rep meshing, physical groups                           | `netgen-mesher` / `gmsh`                          |
| Mesh conversion                          | FEM/CFD format and field exchange                                             | `meshio`                                          |
| Geometry QA                              | Watertightness, 3D manifold booleans, topology, intersections                 | `trimesh, manifold3d, shapely, rtree`             |
| 3D simulation images                     | Mesh/scalar fields, slices, streamlines, PNG screenshots                      | `pyvista`                                         |
| Interactive simulation views             | Standalone HTML assets; Model viewers do not execute HTML                     | `plotly`                                          |
| Simulation animations                    | Rendered frame sequences; GIF and MP4 through the bundled encoder             | `imageio, imageio-ffmpeg`                         |
| Point-cloud registration                 | Denoise, align and compare scans                                              | `open3d, laspy`                                   |
| GIS / site data                          | Vector queries, coordinate systems                                            | `geopandas, pyproj`                               |
| Terrain rasters                          | DEM and geospatial raster I/O                                                 | `rasterio`                                        |
| Section properties                       | Area, inertia, torsion, warping, plastic moduli                               | `sectionproperties`                               |
| Frame / truss / plate FEA                | Member forces, reactions, deflection, P–Delta, tension/compression-only       | `PyNiteFEA`                                       |
| Structural modes / linear buckling       | Generalized eigenmodes and linearized stability                               | `scikit-fem, scipy`                               |
| Geotechnical springs                     | Idealized Winkler foundation, mat subgrade and nodal spring response          | `PyNiteFEA, scipy`                                |
| Multibody dynamics / flexible contact    | Rigid/flexible bodies, joints, collisions, nonlinear time-history integration | `exudyn`                                          |
| Custom FEM / 3D linear elasticity        | Weak forms, 3D linear stress and modal prototypes                             | `scikit-fem`                                      |
| Nonlinear 3D solid mechanics (prototype) | Large deformations, hyperelasticity, automatic differentiation, continuation  | `felupe, scikit-fem`                              |
| Sparse PDE linear systems                | Krylov solvers, sparse assembly and multigrid preconditioning                 | `scipy, pyamg`                                    |
| Optimized numerical kernels              | JIT-compile custom CPU numerical loops                                        | `numba, numpy`                                    |
| Fatigue screening                        | Rainflow cycles, S–N life, cumulative damage                                  | `pylife, rainflow`                                |
| Structural criterion checks              | Evaluate engineer-approved allowables                                         | `numpy, pint`                                     |
| Topology prototypes                      | Explore candidate layouts, not final designs                                  | `scikit-fem, pymoo`                               |
| Pipe / duct sizing                       | Pressure drops, friction, flow correlations                                   | `fluids, scipy`                                   |
| Incompressible CFD                       | 2D/3D Navier—Stokes, velocity and pressure fields                             | `phiflow`                                         |
| Lattice Boltzmann CFD                    | 1D/2D/3D numerical flow simulations                                           | `pylbm`                                           |
| CFD-to-heat prototype                    | Script fluid boundary fields into solid heat PDE                              | `phiflow, FiPy`                                   |
| Heat exchangers                          | Heat-transfer correlations and sizing                                         | `ht, fluids`                                      |
| Fluid properties                         | Enthalpy, density, phase properties                                           | `CoolProp, thermo`                                |
| Refrigeration / heat pumps               | Refrigerant cycle and state calculations                                      | `CoolProp, ht`                                    |
| Ground-source heat pumps                 | Borehole field thermal response                                               | `pygfunction`                                     |
| Psychrometrics                           | Dew point, humidity, moist-air enthalpy                                       | `psychrolib, CoolProp`                            |
| Transient heat / transport PDE           | Finite-volume diffusion, advection and reaction terms                         | `FiPy`                                            |
| Reaction kinetics / combustion           | Chemical equilibrium, species, reactors                                       | `cantera`                                         |
| Smoke tracer prototype                   | Advection—diffusion of prescribed species (not fire CFD)                      | `FiPy`                                            |
| Room acoustics                           | Reverberation, impulse responses                                              | `pyroomacoustics`                                 |
| Water networks                           | Pipe flow, pressure and network quality                                       | `wntr`                                            |
| Stormwater / sewer hydraulics            | Rainfall, runoff, routing and sewer flows                                     | `pyswmm, swmm-toolkit`                            |
| Groundwater time-series                  | Simulate and calibrate groundwater heads over time                            | `pastas`                                          |
| Groundwater PDE (prototype)              | Script Darcy flow with prescribed hydraulic coefficients                      | `scikit-fem, scipy`                               |
| Flood modelling (2D)                     | Shallow-water overland depth, velocity, extent                                | `landlab` ; `anuga` is an excluded optional extra |
| Bridge scour screening                   | Calculate approved empirical envelopes                                        | `numpy, scipy`                                    |
| Solar PV                                 | Irradiance and photovoltaic yield                                             | `pvlib`                                           |
| Solar shadow screening                   | Solar positions and ray/geometry intersection                                 | `pvlib, trimesh, manifold3d`                      |
| Daylight simulation                      | Ray-traced illuminance, daylight factor and glare metrics                     | `pyradiance`                                      |
| Simple building thermal model            | Scripted thermal RC-network energy balances                                   | `scipy, control`                                  |
| Whole-building energy simulation         | Dynamic multizone building energy and HVAC simulation                         | `pyenergyplus-lbnl`                               |
| Battery simulation                       | Cell electrochemistry, charge/discharge and aging models                      | `pybamm`                                          |
| RF / microwave networks                  | S-parameters, signal-chain and transmission-line analysis                     | `scikit-rf`                                       |
| Electromagnetic fields (prototype)       | 3D Maxwell FDTD wave propagation                                              | `fdtd`                                            |
| Electrical power flow                    | AC/DC networks and faults                                                     | `pandapower`                                      |
| Energy-grid optimization                 | Generation, storage, LP/MILP dispatch studies                                 | `pypsa, highspy`                                  |
| Controls                                 | State space, stability and response                                           | `control, scipy`                                  |
| Sensor analysis                          | Filter, align and assess time series                                          | `pandas, scipy`                                   |
| Sensitivity                              | Sobol, Morris and input influence                                             | `SALib`                                           |
| Uncertainty / reliability                | Uncertainty propagation and reliability                                       | `openturns`                                       |
| Constrained optimization                 | LP/MILP/QP/conic solvers and multiobjective Pareto search                     | `scipy, highspy, clarabel, pymoo`                 |
| Multidisciplinary optimization           | Coupled models and derivatives                                                | `openmdao`                                        |
| One-way fluid-to-structure prototype     | Apply computed fluid loads to scripted elastic model                          | `phiflow, scikit-fem`                             |
| Manufacturability screening              | Offsets, thickness and manifold geometry checks                               | `build123d, trimesh, manifold3d`                  |
| Scan-based inspection                    | Compare measured cloud with model                                             | `open3d, laspy`                                   |
| Units / dimensions                       | Convert quantities, detect unit errors                                        | `pint`                                            |
| Basis / evidence schema                  | Implement typed records and validation                                        | `pydantic`                                        |
| T0–T3 scoring                            | Implement evidence levels and dependency caps                                 | `pydantic, networkx`                              |
| Content-addressed evidence               | Canonical JSON and cryptographic hashes                                       | `rfc8785` (plus stdlib `hashlib`)                 |
| Provenance                               | Trace sources, calculations and dependencies                                  | `prov, networkx`                                  |
| Portable evidence packages               | Export interoperable research records                                         | `rocrate`                                         |
| Digital signatures                       | Sign and verify evidence payloads                                             | `cryptography`                                    |
| Reproducible workflows                   | Execute analysis DAGs and reruns                                              | `snakemake`                                       |
| Verification tests                       | Benchmarks, property tests and regressions                                    | `pytest, hypothesis, pytest-benchmark`            |
| Engineering reports / 2D plots           | Graphs, heatmaps, PDF, DOCX and spreadsheets                                  | `matplotlib, typst, python-docx, openpyxl`        |

This is a capability map for the declared library families, not a claim that every workflow is a turnkey solver. The project includes these families in the shared base environment. ANUGA (`flood-gpl`) is optional and excluded from both standard desktop and server profiles. Consult the selected package’s own license and API when preparing a worker or distributing results.

## Visual Results and Runtime Limits [#visual-results-and-runtime-limits]

Use [Matplotlib](https://matplotlib.org/stable/users/explain/figure/backends.html) with `Agg` for PNG/SVG charts, and [PyVista](https://docs.pyvista.org/) for off-screen mesh/field screenshots. Plotly can generate standalone HTML; [Kaleido static export requires Chrome/Chromium](https://plotly.com/python/static-image-export/), which is not a dependency of this Python profile.

Jobs run in worker processes with network, subprocess and sensitive-host-path guards. The process adapter permits the locked environment’s bundled FFmpeg, Radiance and EnergyPlus executables; arbitrary shell commands, Python child processes and network sockets remain blocked. Snakemake workflows that launch arbitrary external commands require a separate worker. Use `from Pynite import FEModel3D` for PyNiteFEA and `import phi` for PhiFlow; their distribution names differ from their import names.

Headless Linux images also need the native shared libraries required by their wheels, including OpenGL/X11 and OpenMP where applicable. Open3D’s Linux wheels require a sufficiently new glibc. Large native stacks belong in container-backed workers rather than ordinary Lambda zip deployments. These constraints are part of deployment verification, not capabilities Python dependencies alone can guarantee.

The numerical libraries enable custom finite-element, finite-volume, CFD, thermal and optimization workflows. They do not supply a validated general industrial turbulence, plasticity/contact, aquifer, fire or two-way fluid/structure solver. Define inputs, units, mesh, boundary conditions and numerical methods explicitly; check convergence and benchmark results before using them for engineering decisions. Library availability indicates computability, not physical validation, standards compliance or an authorized design release.


# SQLite Runner (/ar/docs/automation/sqlite-runner)



Scopture exposes the relational contents of a `.duc` drawing through `ducpy.DucSQL`. Use MCP `run_sqlite` for remote drawings, or CLI `run-sql` for a local file or remote drawing ID. Both remote interfaces use the same validated backend operation.

Resolve a named drawing with `list_available_drawings` before querying it. See the [Duc SQL schema](https://ducflair.github.io/duc/reference/sql/) for the drawing database model; inspect available tables and columns rather than assuming application database tables exist inside a `.duc` file.

## Read One or More Drawings [#read-one-or-more-drawings]

Send tool arguments like these to `run_sqlite`:

```json
{
  "drawingIds": ["drawing-a", "drawing-b"],
  "mode": "per-drawing",
  "query": "SELECT id, type FROM {db}.elements WHERE type = ?",
  "parameters": ["model"],
  "maxRows": 100,
  "waitForCompletionMs": 0
}
```

`per-drawing` runs the query separately against each drawing. Bare table names also work. `{db}` expands to the current database alias; returned rows include their drawing identity. The runner opens drawing databases sequentially, and `maxRows` limits the combined result across the request.

Use `PRAGMA {db}.table_info(elements)` to inspect columns or `SELECT name FROM {db}.sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table'` to inspect tables. Read modes accept `SELECT`, `WITH`, and read-only `PRAGMA`; database connections also enforce read-only access.

## Join Drawings [#join-drawings]

Use `attached` mode and explicit SQL-safe aliases when a query needs more than one drawing at once:

```json
{
  "drawingIds": ["drawing-a", "drawing-b"],
  "mode": "attached",
  "aliases": {"drawing-a": "source", "drawing-b": "reference"},
  "query": "SELECT s.id FROM source.elements s JOIN reference.elements r ON s.id = r.id",
  "maxRows": 100
}
```

Without custom aliases, the runner derives them from drawing IDs as `db_<drawingId>`, replacing unsupported characters with underscores and resolving duplicates. Use the returned `drawings` metadata to identify each alias.

## Apply a Change [#apply-a-change]

`mutate` accepts exactly one drawing and requires edit access and execution permission. Use unqualified table names and bind values with `parameters`:

```json
{
  "drawingIds": ["drawing-a"],
  "mode": "mutate",
  "query": "UPDATE elements SET label = ? WHERE id = ?",
  "parameters": ["Revised mount", "element-id"],
  "waitForCompletionMs": 0
}
```

Mutations are persisted through Scopture’s drawing update and versioning path. Read the targeted records first and verify them afterward. Remote Issues and Charter records are managed through their own tools; changing drawing SQL does not replace those services, and deletion of Issues or Charter items must be done manually in Scopture.

## Limits and Background Jobs [#limits-and-background-jobs]

| Setting          | Limit                                                       |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `per-drawing`    | 100 drawing IDs per request                                 |
| `attached`       | 10 distinct drawing IDs, matching SQLite’s attachment limit |
| `mutate`         | One drawing ID                                              |
| `maxRows`        | 500 by default; at most 5,000 combined rows                 |
| Query size       | 100,000 characters                                          |
| Bound parameters | At most 100 strings, numbers, booleans, or nulls            |

A request creates one job. Server jobs wait in a durable queue with at most four concurrent workers. Jobs for the same user and organization run one at a time; additional requests do not start an unbounded number of Python processes. Large drawings and attached joins still consume more worker time and memory, so select the necessary fields and use result limits.

`waitForCompletionMs` defaults to `0`: submission returns a `jobId` promptly. Poll it with `check_python_run_job`, for example:

```json
{"jobId": "returned-job-id", "waitForCompletionMs": 10000}
```

Keep polling the same ID while its status is `queued`, `running`, or `applying`. A short HTTP wait is separate from the worker runtime; a pending job continues after the response. Do not resubmit a pending mutation. Each HTTP polling call waits at most 20 seconds, including the time already spent preparing that request, while a server worker can execute for up to 15 minutes. Jobs expire after 24 hours.

If submission finishes during its requested wait, `run_sqlite.result` contains `columns`, `rows`, `rowCount`, `truncated`, and drawing aliases. Otherwise, the completed job’s stdout contains the same result after the `__SCOPTURE_RUN_SQLITE_RESULT__` marker. Failed jobs include an error; read-only SQL jobs can be polled with read access.

## CLI Examples [#cli-examples]

```bash
scopture run-sql ./assembly.duc "SELECT id, type FROM elements" --raw
scopture run-sql <drawing-id> "SELECT id, type FROM elements" --raw
scopture run-sql ./assembly.duc "UPDATE elements SET label = 'Mount' WHERE id = 'element-id'" --mutate
```

Local files run on the device. Remote drawing IDs use the backend and the CLI polls the submitted job. Multi-drawing aliases, bound parameters, and row limits are exposed by MCP `run_sqlite`; consult `scopture run-sql --help` for the installed CLI’s options.

See [MCP Tool](/docs/automation/mcp-tool), [CLI Tool](/docs/automation/cli-tool), and [Python Sandbox](/docs/automation/python-sandbox) for setup and the broader execution model.


# Canvas and Artifacts (/ar/docs/concepts/canvas-and-artifacts)



## The Canvas as a Review Surface [#the-canvas-as-a-review-surface]

Scopture opens a drawing as an infinite canvas where project artifacts can be arranged beside the requirements, explanations, and review activity that qualify them. The canvas is the shared application surface for drawing, navigation, inspection, and collaboration; it is not a replacement for the specialist tools that authored the source material.

Use Scopture’s search, layers, groups, grids, snapping, measurements, and unit controls to move between the overview of a project and the detail being reviewed. Frames provide named visual regions, while plots identify deliberate output areas for presentation and export.

## Working with Artifacts [#working-with-artifacts]

Scopture can place 2D geometry, annotations, images, PDFs, documents, web references, and engineering models in the same drawing. In the application, the important distinction is how each artifact participates in review:

| Review need                  | Scopture behavior                                                                               |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Explain or mark up           | Draw, measure, label, connect, and annotate directly on the canvas                              |
| Provide evidence             | Position source sheets, reports, images, documents, and references beside the work they support |
| Inspect engineering geometry | Open a model element in its dedicated interactive environment                                   |
| Organize the review          | Use frames, layers, groups, and search to control context and navigation                        |
| Prepare an output            | Use plots or a selected canvas region to define what should be exported                         |

The underlying element types, relationships, and storage rules belong to the Duc format. See [Elements](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/elements/overview), [Document Elements](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/elements/document-element), [Plot Elements](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/elements/plot-element), and [Blocks](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/elements/blocks) in the Duc documentation.

## Model Review in Scopture [#model-review-in-scopture]

On the canvas, a model remains positioned alongside the rest of the project context. Its thumbnail represents the current generated output. Opening it in **Model Open mode** selects the viewer recorded in that output: parametric or IFC 3D, DXF 2D, image, SVG, PDF, or table. The element keeps its identity and canvas position when the output type changes.

The 3D viewer provides model selection, hierarchy navigation, camera controls, measurement, sectioning, display and material controls, and saved viewpoints. PDF output provides page navigation, while image, SVG, and table outputs open in their corresponding viewers.

Python models declare their result with `emit_output(...)`. Scopture stores the generated bytes as a referenced external file, together with the output kind, content and input fingerprints, and generation metadata. The properties panel shows **fresh**, **stale**, **missing**, or **failed** output. Changes to source code, parameters, dependency modules, or external inputs trigger cache and thumbnail regeneration when local or authorized cloud execution is available.

An issue created during model inspection can return a reviewer to the relevant model location and viewing context. This connects a detailed geometry discussion back to the same issue and decision workflow used elsewhere in the drawing.

For supported model sources, Python output contracts, external-file relationships, and stored viewer state, see [Model Elements](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/elements/model-element) in the Duc documentation.


# Charter, Issues, and Decisions (/ar/docs/concepts/charter-issues-and-decisions)



## Review Context in the Application [#review-context-in-the-application]

Scopture presents the charter, issues, and decisions beside the drawing they describe. The charter states what the review should evaluate, issues capture what needs attention in the work, and decisions preserve the resolved project direction.

The Duc format defines these records and their relationships. For their fields, statuses, anchor structures, and format-level traceability model, see [Charter & Issues](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/charter-and-issues) in the Duc documentation.

## Start with the Charter [#start-with-the-charter]

Open the charter before arranging or reviewing project evidence. In Scopture, it provides the maintained brief for the drawing: its objective, current phase, requirements, constraints, responsible stakeholders, and recorded decisions.

Keeping this context visible allows reviewers to judge an artifact against stated acceptance conditions instead of reconstructing intent from filenames, annotations, or messages.

## Capture Issues Where They Occur [#capture-issues-where-they-occur]

Create an issue from the canvas or during model inspection so the discussion retains its visual context. Scopture can return participants to the relevant canvas position, element, or model location rather than relying on a detached written description.

Use the issue thread for discussion and supporting material, then manage the same issue set through the list, board, or timeline according to the review task. Assignments, followers, reminders, and due dates help coordinate action without changing what the issue refers to.

## Carry the Outcome into a Decision [#carry-the-outcome-into-a-decision]

Closing an issue records that its immediate review work is complete. When the outcome changes or confirms the project direction, record the result as a charter decision and link the issues that informed it.

A practical Scopture workflow is:

1. Review an artifact against the charter.
2. Anchor an issue at the source of a question or requested change.
3. Resolve the discussion in the issue thread.
4. Record a consequential outcome as a linked decision.
5. Preserve the accepted drawing state with a checkpoint.

This keeps the application focused on the review process while Duc preserves the portable relationships underneath it.


# Drawings, Sharing, and Export (/ar/docs/concepts/drawings-sharing-and-export)



## Local and Remote Drawings [#local-and-remote-drawings]

Scopture supports desktop local files and remote drawings with the same underlying `.duc` project state:

| Feature             | Local drawing                                        | Remote drawing                                                                            |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Primary storage** | A real `.duc` file on the desktop filesystem         | Scopture cloud storage within an organization                                             |
| **Offline work**    | Solo desktop editing and native Python execution     | Temporary local recovery state; shared operations and remote compute require connectivity |
| **Collaboration**   | Single-device working state                          | Live collaborators, presence, shared issues, and managed access                           |
| **Access**          | Controlled by access to the device and exported file | Controlled through roles, direct access, organization access, and public links            |

A local drawing can be moved to the cloud when the drawing and its required assets are available for upload. A local filesystem path does not grant the cloud access to that file.

### Client Access [#client-access]

| Client and drawing                                     | Editing and saves                                    |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Desktop local drawing                                  | Solo editing; filesystem `.duc` saves                |
| Free browser access to public or community drawings    | Read-only                                            |
| Browser local file                                     | Read-only; no offline editing or durable local saves |
| Mobile local folders and `.duc` files                  | Read-only                                            |
| Authenticated paid cloud drawing on a supported client | Cloud editing with the required drawing permission   |

Cloud access follows the plan of the drawing’s organization. A public link alone does not enable editing or compute.

## Local Saves and Recovery [#local-saves-and-recovery]

New desktop local drawings receive a `.duc` file in Scopture’s application data directory. **Reveal source in folder** opens the file’s location. **Save As** writes the drawing to a chosen path and updates the source location after the save succeeds.

Autosave and explicit saves write the native file. Scopture also keeps temporary state in the Origin Private File System (OPFS) for autosave recovery and reconciliation. This recovery copy is separate from the durable `.duc` file.

When a native file is reopened with pending recovered edits, Scopture offers **Restore recovered changes** or **Open saved file**. If another application or window changed the file on disk, Scopture refuses to overwrite that newer content until the states are reconciled. Keep a separate copy with **Save As** when both versions are needed.

On macOS, right-click Scopture’s Dock icon for **Open Recent** and **New Window**. Each window has its own drawing and menu actions.

***

## Workspace Organization [#workspace-organization]

The dashboard is the project entry point outside the canvas. It surfaces recent drawings and issue activity, while the file explorer organizes remote drawings in nested folders and provides search, movement, and trash recovery. Organization membership determines which shared workspace and files a person can reach.

Local drawings remain listed as device-resident work. They should not be treated as shared cloud files until they are explicitly moved to a remote workspace.

***

## External Files [#external-files]

When a drawing uses a PDF, image, document, spreadsheet, or engineering model, Scopture resolves the asset when it is displayed, reviewed, or exported. Desktop offline drawings can **Embed a copy** or **Link local file** when choosing a supported asset.

An embedded copy travels inside the saved `.duc`. A local link stores an explicit relative or absolute locator and omits that revision’s bytes from the native file. Relative links resolve against the owning `.duc` directory. **Save As** rebases them to keep pointing to the same files. Absolute links keep their native target path.

Local links require native permission to read the target. A missing or inaccessible reference offers **Locate file**, which lets you choose the replacement and grant access. Changes to a linked source update its input revision so dependent model output can regenerate. Carry linked files with the drawing, or embed them, when handing the project to another device. Local links are restricted to desktop offline drawings and are not mounted in remote Python jobs.

The storage structure, external-file identity, revisions, and active payload selection are defined by Duc rather than the Scopture interface. See [External Files & Revisions](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/external-files) for those mechanics.

***

## Access and Collaboration [#access-and-collaboration]

Remote drawings support live presence and synchronized editing, including shared navigation and model-review context. Access can be granted directly to a person, inherited through an organization role, or provided through a public link.

Workspace permissions distinguish **view**, **comment**, **edit**, and **full** access. Effective editing also requires authentication and an entitled paid cloud plan. Public-link settings can additionally control:

* password protection;
* whether export is allowed;
* whether interactive 3D mode is available; and
* whether an unprotected drawing can be discovered.

Authenticated access takes precedence when a participant already has a stronger direct or organization permission. Use named access for ongoing collaborators and public links for clearly bounded external reviews.

***

## Import and Export [#import-and-export]

Scopture can export a portable `.duc` drawing or produce presentation and interchange outputs for narrower purposes:

* canvas, selection, view, crop, or plot output as PNG, SVG, or PDF;
* a text-based drawing representation when structured inspection is needed;
* supported engineering-model outputs whose available formats depend on the model type; and
* the source representation of supported code-generated models.

An image or PDF export communicates a view. A model export communicates geometry. A `.duc` export is intended for continuing with the drawing and its project context. Choose the output according to what the recipient must inspect or continue editing.

For what the portable file contains and how it is structured, see the [Duc architecture](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/architecture).

<Callout type="warn" title="Sharing and export are separate permissions">
  Access to a public drawing does not necessarily allow its assets to be exported or its models to be opened in 3D. Configure those capabilities explicitly for the review being shared.
</Callout>


# Model Parameters (/ar/docs/concepts/model-parameters)





## Parameters as a Workflow Interface [#parameters-as-a-workflow-interface]

Python Model Elements can expose selected source values as controls in Scopture’s **Parameters** panel. This turns the model’s Python source into a focused interface: a reviewer or designer can adjust the values that define an option without editing the rest of the implementation.

Parameters are most effective when they represent design intent rather than incidental implementation details. Dimensions, clearances, counts, labels, and font choices are good candidates because they can be named, reviewed, and changed independently from the geometry that consumes them.

```python
width = 120
height = 80
wall_thickness = 5
show_fasteners = True
project_label = "North Wing"
FONTS = FontEnum(["Inter", "Roboto"])
```

When Scopture recognizes these declarations, it presents suitable controls for numeric values, Boolean values, text, and font lists. Boolean literals (`True` and `False`) appear as switches. Selecting a Python Model Element exposes its detected parameters in the properties sidebar. Selecting a plot can expose parameters from Python Model Elements nested within that plot, making the plot a practical control surface for the option it presents.

<img alt="Detected Python model parameters in Scopture's properties sidebar, controlling fonts, dimensions, and text on a 3D model" src="__img0" />

## Authoring Detectable Parameters [#authoring-detectable-parameters]

Keep editable declarations at the top level and assign literal values directly to named variables:

```python
panel_width: float = 120.0
panel_count = 6
show_fasteners: bool = True
system_name = "South facade"
```

Derive computed values below the editable declarations:

```python
panel_width = 120.0
panel_count = 6

array_width = panel_width * panel_count
```

The panel is intentionally conservative. Assignments inside functions or classes, comments, docstrings, computed expressions, formatted strings, and complex data structures are not treated as editable parameters. Font collections should use a clearly named top-level list or tuple such as `fonts`, `font_families`, or `typefaces`; `FontEnum(...)` is also supported.

Parameter edits update the corresponding literal in the Model Element’s Python source, so the code remains the authoritative and portable representation of the design.

## Combine Parameters with Modular Models [#combine-parameters-with-modular-models]

A strong pattern is to place shared parameters in a logic-only Model Element and import them into one or more rendering elements. The parameter element does not need to display geometry.

```python
# Parameter element ID: mmBUBjTesxYfxL0HDjXWg
width = 120
height = 80
wall_thickness = 5
```

```python
# Rendering element
from duc_model.mmBUBjTesxYfxL0HDjXWg import width, height, wall_thickness
from build123d import Box

wall = Box(width, wall_thickness, height)
emit_output(wall, kind="parametric")
```

When a shared value changes, Scopture marks dependent output as stale. With execution available, it regenerates the model cache, saves the output artifact, and updates the thumbnail in the background. Desktop uses its native Python sandbox for both local and remote drawings; browser and mobile use the authorized paid cloud sandbox. See [Python Sandbox](/docs/automation/python-sandbox) for execution contexts, available packages and runtime limits. A parameter module can therefore drive several coordinated views or assemblies.

A current saved artifact can be displayed when a drawing reopens without executing its Python again. The declared output selects the viewer, so the same Model Element can produce CAD, DXF, an image, SVG, PDF, or a table. See [Model Elements](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/elements/model-element) for `emit_output(...)` and the stored output contract.

Use the model import completion list in the Python editor to insert the stable module reference. The visible model label helps identify the source, while the element ID provides the durable reference used by the import.

For the underlying module identity, import forms, remapping behavior, and dependency-graph contract, see [Model Element Modularization](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/model-modularization) in the Duc documentation.

## Recommended Workflow [#recommended-workflow]

1. Create a Python Model Element for the values that should be editable.
2. Declare those values as simple numeric, boolean, text, or font-list literals.
3. Import the values from `duc_model.<model-element-id>` in the elements that consume them.
4. Call `emit_output(...)` once in the rendering root. Parameter and helper modules should expose their values and functions.
5. Select the parameter element or its containing plot and iterate from the **Parameters** panel.

This structure keeps the editable interface small, the Python implementation modular, and the downstream effects of each design change explicit.


# Versions and Revisions (/ar/docs/concepts/versions-and-revisions)



## Drawing History in Scopture [#drawing-history-in-scopture]

Scopture exposes a drawing’s history so reviewers can preserve milestones, inspect earlier states, and recover from an unwanted change. Create a named checkpoint before a formal review, approval, handoff, major import, or other boundary that should remain easy to identify.

Name the event or accepted state rather than the person who created it, for example, “Coordination review accepted” or “Before structural model revision.”

## Preview Before Restoring [#preview-before-restoring]

Preview a historical state to confirm that it contains the intended drawing, project context, and referenced artifacts. Restore it only when the active drawing should continue from that point. Restoration is permission-controlled and is different from ordinary canvas undo.

Scopture also records bounded background and agent operations in drawing history. This makes an automated change inspectable and recoverable through the same application workflow as other project changes.

Desktop file recovery is separate from drawing history. The `.duc` file is the durable local save; temporary application storage retains pending edits for crash recovery. When reopening a file with pending edits, choose whether to restore the recovered state or open the saved file. See [Local Saves and Recovery](/docs/concepts/drawings-sharing-and-export#local-saves-and-recovery).

## Source-File Revisions [#source-file-revisions]

A source-file revision and a drawing-history entry serve different review tasks. Replacing or revising an IFC, STEP, DXF, PDF, or other referenced asset updates the source being examined; a drawing checkpoint preserves the broader Scopture context around it.

Keep the revised source associated with the same review narrative, then create a checkpoint when the project reaches a meaningful state. Existing issues and decisions can then be evaluated against the changed artifact without treating its context as disposable.

The version graph, checkpoints, deltas, restoration rules, external-file records, and active revision mechanics are Duc format concerns. See [Version Control](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/version-control) and [External Files & Revisions](https://duc.ducflair.com/docs/concepts/external-files) for those details.


# Run a Design Review (/ar/docs/get-started/design-review)



## 1. Choose the Drawing Mode [#1-choose-the-drawing-mode]

Start with a **remote drawing** for shared review and collaboration. Editing and remote compute require authentication, a paid organization plan, and the relevant drawing permissions. Free browser access is read-only.

Use a **local drawing in the desktop app** for solo offline work. The drawing is saved as a `.duc` file on disk. Local files opened on mobile are read-only. Before moving a local drawing to the cloud, make its linked assets available for upload.

Both modes use the same Scopture canvas and `.duc` project state.

***

## 2. State the Review Intent [#2-state-the-review-intent]

Open the charter before arranging the review material. Record only the context that determines how the work should be evaluated:

* the objective and current phase;
* requirements and their acceptance criteria;
* hard or soft constraints;
* responsible stakeholders; and
* decisions that have already been made.

The charter is the stable project brief. It prevents reviewers from having to reconstruct intent from annotations, messages, or filenames.

***

## 3. Assemble the Evidence [#3-assemble-the-evidence]

Bring only the material needed to understand the review. Scopture can combine 2D geometry and annotations with PDFs, documents, images, links, and engineering models such as IFC, STEP, STL, DXF, and DWG.

Use frames to establish visual sections, plots to define deliberate output regions, layers to control visibility, and blocks for content that should be reused consistently. Keep source artifacts near the references and explanations that qualify them.

***

## 4. Inspect in Context [#4-inspect-in-context]

Review the drawing at the level appropriate to the question. The canvas supports measurement, snapping, search, layers, and multiple unit scopes. Model elements can be opened in an interactive viewer for selection, hierarchy inspection, measurement, sectioning, material and display controls, and saved viewpoints.

The canvas view explains how an artifact relates to the project. Model Open mode selects the viewer for the current output: 3D, DXF, image, SVG, PDF, or table.

***

## 5. Capture Issues at the Source [#5-capture-issues-at-the-source]

Create an issue where the question occurs. An issue can point to:

* a position on the canvas;
* a particular element and a local position on that element; or
* a point in a 3D model, including its orientation, model identity, and viewer state.

Give the issue a clear outcome to resolve, then use its thread for evidence, replies, attachments, assignments, followers, and timing. Anchoring the discussion removes ambiguity when the canvas or model is revisited later.

***

## 6. Resolve and Preserve [#6-resolve-and-preserve]

Close or dismiss issues deliberately. When an outcome changes the project direction, record it as a charter decision with its rationale and link the issues that informed it.

Create a named checkpoint before a formal review, handoff, or major revision. Checkpoints preserve complete project states; the version graph also records incremental changes between them. Preview a historical state before restoring it.

***

## 7. Share the Right Surface [#7-share-the-right-surface]

For remote drawings, grant direct or organization access when participants need an ongoing role. Use a public link for a bounded review. A viewer can edit only when their authentication, plan, and drawing permission allow it. Public links can also require a password and independently control export, 3D access, and discoverability.

The review is complete when its intent, evidence, unresolved issues, resolved decisions, and accepted state can be understood without reconstructing them from another system.


# Tutorials (/ar/docs/get-started/tutorials)



Use these tutorials to follow Scopture workflows from the interface. The collection is updated as new guides become available.

<DocsTutorials />


# What Is Scopture? (/ar/docs/get-started/what-is-scopture)



Scopture connects engineering outputs on an infinite canvas, makes them reviewable in two and three dimensions, and records what was requested, questioned, decided, and changed.

## What Scopture Keeps Together [#what-scopture-keeps-together]

| Project context   | Purpose                                                                                       |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Artifacts**     | Drawings, interactive models, PDFs, documents, images, references, and reusable blocks        |
| **Intent**        | The project charter, including objectives, requirements, constraints, stakeholders, and phase |
| **Review**        | Issues anchored to a canvas location, an element, or an exact point in a 3D model             |
| **Decisions**     | Outcomes and rationale linked back to the issues that informed them                           |
| **History**       | Checkpoints, incremental changes, external-file revisions, previews, and restoration          |
| **Collaboration** | Live presence, comments, assignments, controlled sharing, and review permissions              |

The result is a navigable record of the project state and the reasoning around it, rather than a folder of disconnected deliverables.

## Local and Remote Drawings [#local-and-remote-drawings]

Use a **remote drawing** when the work must be shared, reviewed in a browser, or edited with live collaborators. Cloud editing and compute require authentication, an entitled paid organization, and the relevant drawing permissions. Free browser access supports read-only public and community drawings.

Use a **local drawing in the desktop app** for solo offline editing. Scopture saves a real `.duc` file on disk, supports linked local assets, and runs Python locally. Mobile opens local folders and `.duc` files read-only, without local Python or AI. A local drawing can be moved to the cloud when its assets are available for upload.

See [Drawings, Sharing, and Export](/docs/concepts/drawings-sharing-and-export) for storage, recovery, and access details. The desktop app also includes a [command-line interface](/docs/automation/cli-tool).

## Product Boundary [#product-boundary]

Scopture does not replace the specialist tools used to author engineering geometry, run discipline-specific analysis, or manage construction and production. It is the decision-traceability layer between design creation and execution: the place where heterogeneous evidence can be assembled, examined, discussed, and approved without losing its relationships.

Continue with [Run a Design Review](/docs/get-started/design-review) to see how that context is used in practice.


# Scopture Docs (/hi/docs)





<img alt="An engineering model open for interactive inspection in Scopture" src="__img0" />

> An engineering model open for interactive inspection in Scopture, , representing physical-engineering work from the <a href="http://oresat.org/satellites/oresat0-5" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" className="underline hover:text-fd-foreground">OreSat 0.5</a> project.

Scopture is a desktop and cloud workspace for reviewing physical-engineering work before it is executed. It brings drawings, interactive models, references, issues, decisions, and revision history into one shared context, so the reasoning behind a design remains available as the design changes.

The desktop app supports solo offline editing with real `.duc` files and local Python execution. Authenticated paid cloud workspaces support remote editing and compute with the required permissions. Free browser access and local files opened on mobile are read-only.

Teams continue to create source material in the CAD, BIM, analysis, and authoring tools suited to their disciplines. Scopture provides the review and decision-traceability layer between that work and physical execution.
